# **AI Fraud-Review Copilot**

## **Problem & Domain**

Fraud and risk teams at banks and fintechs flag transactions with rule-based triggers — unusual amount, new merchant category, geographic anomaly, velocity spikes. Every flag then lands on an analyst's desk, who manually pulls the customer's transaction history, checks the merchant's reputation, and writes a case note recommending escalation or clearance. This manual triage is slow, inconsistent in format, and doesn't scale with flag volume — a well-documented bottleneck in fraud operations.

**Target user:** the fraud/risk analyst who currently writes this note by hand, and indirectly the compliance team that needs consistent, auditable reasoning behind every decision.

**One-line solution:** an agent that, given a flagged transaction, retrieves the relevant fraud-pattern knowledge, pulls customer and merchant context through tool calls, and drafts a structured case note with a recommendation — always routed to a human for the final call.

## **Scope for the Week**

**In scope:**

* Synthetic transaction/customer/merchant data (generated by you — no real financial data, no PII risk)  
* Simple rule-based flagging (amount spike, new merchant category, geo anomaly, velocity)  
* A small fraud-pattern knowledge base, retrieved via RAG  
* Two tool calls: customer history lookup, merchant info lookup  
* An agent that drafts a structured case note with a recommendation  
* One guardrail: no definitive fraud claims, PII redaction in any output  
* A 15–20 case eval set with known ground truth  
* An API, containerized and deployed, with CI/CD running the eval set on every push

**Out of scope:**

* Real financial data or any real customer PII  
* Training an actual fraud-detection model  
* A frontend UI beyond a simple API (and optionally one HTML page)  
* Multi-analyst collaboration, auth, or production-grade access control

## **Architecture & Components**

![architecture · 5 stages][image1]

architecture · 5 stages

Automated end to end except the last step — the analyst always makes the final call, the agent only drafts the recommendation.

| Component | What it does | Suggested tech |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Data generator | Creates synthetic transactions, customers, merchants with realistic fields | Python script → SQLite or CSV |
| Rule-based flagger | Tags a transaction with a flag reason (amount spike, new merchant category, geo anomaly, velocity) | Plain Python, no ML needed |
| Knowledge base | Short docs describing fraud patterns (card-not-present, account takeover, velocity fraud, geo-anomaly) | Markdown files → Chroma vector store |
| Tool calls | lookup\_customer\_history(customer\_id), lookup\_merchant\_info(merchant\_id) | Native function calling, or a small MCP server for the differentiator |
| Agent / generation layer | Retrieves the relevant pattern doc, calls both tools, drafts the case note | Claude API (or your chosen LLM) |
| Guardrail | Redacts card numbers; constrains language to "recommend escalate/clear," never "this is fraud" | Regex/rule checks wrapping the model output |
| API | Accepts a transaction ID, returns the structured case note as JSON | FastAPI |
| Eval harness | Runs the agent against 15–20 labeled cases, scores recommendation accuracy | Python script, run in CI |
| Deployment | Packages and serves the API | Docker → Render / Fly.io / Railway free tier |
| CI/CD | Runs the eval set and basic tests on every push; fails the build if eval score drops | GitHub Actions |
| Observability | Logs each request, response, latency, token cost, and guardrail triggers | Structured logging |

## **Data Design**

| Entity | Key fields |
| :---- | :---- |
| Transaction | id, customer\_id, merchant\_id, amount, timestamp, location, flag\_reason |
| Customer | id, name (synthetic), home\_location, typical\_spend\_range, account\_age\_days |
| Merchant | id, name (synthetic), category, risk\_tier |

## **Solution Design Summary**

| Dimension | Detail |
| :---- | :---- |
| Serving mode | Synchronous — one flagged transaction in, one case note out, within a few seconds |
| Deployment mode | Containerized (Docker), single instance on a free-tier host, dev/prod split via environment variables |
| Success criteria | ≥80% recommendation-direction accuracy on the eval set; correct risk factor cited; 100% guardrail compliance on an adversarial check |
| Monitoring | Log every request/response, latency, and token cost; track eval score over time in CI; alert on a guardrail-trigger spike or eval regression |
| Maintenance | Periodic human spot-check (e.g. 5% of generated notes) to catch drift; re-run the eval set whenever the prompt or knowledge base changes |

## **Action Plan**

A step-by-step breakdown of the Build Plan above — what to actually do, what you're reaching for, and how to think about each step as you do it.

### **Day 1 — Setup & Understanding**

1. **Scope the project to the exact MVP.** *Tools:* none, just a clear head. *Approach:* write down the one-line solution and the in/out-of-scope lists from this doc somewhere visible — pin it, don't let the build wander past it this week.  
2. **Set up the repo and CLAUDE.md.** *Tools:* Git, GitHub, your editor. *Approach:* write CLAUDE.md before any code — it's cheap now and expensive to retrofit; describe the five-stage architecture in it so your AI tool never has to guess the shape of the system.  
3. **Read and note every reference-table topic.** *Tools:* the framework doc, your AI tool to look things up fast. *Approach:* aim for "I could define this in one sentence," not mastery — depth comes later when you actually hit each concept while building.  
4. **Sketch the architecture decisions.** *Tools:* pen and paper or a plain doc. *Approach:* the five stages are already decided (see the diagram above) — your job today is the specifics: which LLM, which vector DB, what the case-note JSON schema looks like.

### **Day 2 — Data & Retrieval**

5. **Write the synthetic data generator.** *Tools:* Python, faker. *Approach:* don't make the data too clean — a few ambiguous or borderline cases now save you a scramble on Day 4 when you need an eval set with real variance.  
6. **Write the rule-based flagger.** *Tools:* plain Python, no ML. *Approach:* keep the rules dumb on purpose (amount over a threshold, new merchant category, etc.) — the flagging isn't the interesting part of this project, the triage agent is.  
7. **Write the fraud-pattern knowledge base.** *Tools:* four or five short markdown files. *Approach:* write these like you're briefing a new analyst — what the pattern looks like, what evidence usually supports it. This is what grounds your agent's reasoning.  
8. **Set up Chroma and embed the docs.** *Tools:* chromadb. *Approach:* get the simplest version working first — one embedding call, one collection, no tuning yet. You're proving the pipe works before you optimize it.  
9. **Tune chunking and test retrieval manually.** *Tools:* a scratch script, a few hand-written test queries. *Approach:* this is where "chunking strategy" stops being a vocabulary word — run a query, look at what comes back, and if it's the wrong document, that's your signal to adjust chunk size or overlap, not a sign something's broken.

### **Day 3 — The Agent Core**

10. **Write the two tool-call functions.** *Tools:* plain Python functions returning dicts/JSON from your synthetic data. *Approach:* keep these deterministic and boring — they're meant to simulate "systems" the model queries, not to do anything clever themselves.  
11. **Wire the agent loop.** *Tools:* the Anthropic (or OpenAI) SDK's native tool-calling. *Approach:* build it as a straight line first — retrieve, call both tools, generate — before adding any branching or retry logic. A working straight line beats a half-working smart loop.  
12. **Design the case-note output format.** *Tools:* a Pydantic model or a JSON schema in the prompt. *Approach:* decide this before you prompt for it — risk factors, evidence, recommendation, confidence — a structured output is what makes the eval set in Day 4 scorable at all.  
13. **Run the agent end-to-end by hand.** *Tools:* a scratch script, 4–5 flagged transactions. *Approach:* read the actual outputs critically here, not just "did it run" — this is your first real signal on whether retrieval and tool context are actually helping the model reason.

### **Day 4 — API, Guardrail & Eval**

14. **Wrap the agent in FastAPI.** *Tools:* fastapi, uvicorn. *Approach:* one endpoint, one job — POST /review/{transaction\_id} in, structured case note out. Resist adding endpoints you don't need yet.  
15. **Write the guardrail.** *Tools:* regex/rule checks on the model's output. *Approach:* write it as a post-check, not just a prompt instruction — prompts get ignored under pressure, a code-level check doesn't. Test it by trying to break it on purpose.  
16. **Build the eval set.** *Tools:* a spreadsheet or JSON file, your own judgment. *Approach:* hand-label 15–20 cases with the recommendation you'd expect and the risk factor that should be cited — tedious, but the single highest-leverage hour of the week for your interview story.  
17. **Write and run the eval script.** *Tools:* Python, pytest or a plain script. *Approach:* score recommendation-direction accuracy first (did it say escalate when it should have) — don't over-engineer the scoring logic, a simple match is enough for a project this size.

### **Day 5 — Ship It**

18. **Write the Dockerfile and build locally.** *Tools:* Docker. *Approach:* get docker build succeeding before you touch deployment — debugging a broken image on a remote host is miserable, debugging it locally is fast.  
19. **Deploy to a free-tier host.** *Tools:* Render, Fly.io, or Railway. *Approach:* deploy the simplest possible version first (even a hello-world endpoint) to confirm the pipeline works, then push your real app — isolates "my deploy config is wrong" from "my app is wrong."  
20. **Set up CI.** *Tools:* GitHub Actions. *Approach:* make the workflow run your Day 4 eval script on every push — the point isn't testing for its own sake, it's that a prompt change that tanks accuracy should fail the build, same as broken code would.  
21. **Split dev/prod config.** *Tools:* environment variables, .env. *Approach:* two sets of config (local .env, deployed host's env vars), real keys never committed — be ready to explain why that split exists if asked.

### **Day 6 — Harden & Study**

22. **Add logging.** *Tools:* Python's logging module. *Approach:* log what you'd actually want to see if this broke in production at 2am — request in, response out, latency, which guardrail (if any) fired.  
23. **Fix what the eval and guardrail testing exposed.** *Tools:* whatever the bug needs. *Approach:* this is real debugging-with-AI practice — paste the actual failing case to your AI tool, not a vague description, and judge its fix rather than accepting it blindly.  
24. **Reread your Day 1 notes on the Know-tier topics.** *Tools:* your own notes. *Approach:* this is a recall check, not new learning — if a term doesn't come back to you quickly, that's exactly what to flashcard for Day 7\.

### **Day 7 — The Pitch**

25. **Write the project narrative.** *Tools:* the Pitch template in the framework doc. *Approach:* write it the way you'd actually say it out loud, not like a report — short, concrete, and willing to name a limitation.  
26. **Prep answers for the Know-tier topics.** *Tools:* your notes. *Approach:* one sentence per topic is the bar — you're not expected to lecture on quantization, you're expected to not freeze when it comes up.  
27. **Rehearse out loud.** *Tools:* yourself, maybe a friend. *Approach:* say the pitch and defend one decision under a pushback question ("why not just fine-tune instead of RAG?") — the first time you say it out loud shouldn't be in the interview.

## **Risks & Mitigations**

| Risk | Mitigation |
| :---- | :---- |
| Synthetic data is too easy — retrieval and recommendations look great but wouldn't generalize | Deliberately include a few ambiguous or borderline cases in both the dataset and the eval set |
| Agent drifts into stating fraud as fact instead of a recommendation | Guardrail check runs on every output before it's returned; test it adversarially |
| Eval set is too small to mean much statistically | Fine for a week-long project — the point is having a harness and a CI gate, not statistical power |
| Scope creep (adding a frontend, more tools, more fraud patterns) eats the week | Everything beyond "Scope for the Week" above waits until after the interview |

## **Elevator Pitch Draft**

Fraud analysts spend significant time manually investigating every flagged transaction — pulling customer history, checking merchant reputation, and writing up a case note by hand. I built an agent that does that first pass automatically: it retrieves the relevant fraud pattern, pulls customer and merchant context through tool calls, and drafts a structured case note with a recommendation — but it never makes the final call itself, that stays with a human. It's deployed behind an API, evaluated against a labeled test set on every code change through CI, and guardrailed so it can't state a fraud conclusion as fact or leak card data.

This is a starting draft — refine it with your own specifics once you've built it, then move it into the Pitch template in the main framework doc.

**On CLAUDE.md specifically**, since you asked: it's a plain markdown file your AI coding tool reads for context on every session. A good one for this project covers, in a few short paragraphs: what the project does and why; the architecture at a glance (the five stages); where things live (src/, data/, eval/); how to run it locally; and any conventions you want kept, e.g. "always run python eval/run\_eval.py before committing a prompt or retrieval change."

## **What You'll Witness Along the Way**

* Writing your first CLAUDE.md and noticing your AI tool's answers get sharper once it has project context  
* Your first successful LLM API call — a raw response coming back from the model  
* Chroma returning the wrong document chunk for a query, and tuning chunk size until it returns the right one  
* Watching the model decide to call a tool mid-response, and its return value feed back into what the model says next  
* Deliberately trying to break your own guardrail — asking the agent to just state "this is fraud" — and watching it hold or fail  
* Running your eval script for the first time and getting a real accuracy number instead of a guess  
* docker build — watching layers build, and probably hitting at least one dependency error the first time through  
* docker run, then curling your own API running inside a container for the first time  
* Opening your first real pull request against your own repo, with an actual description  
* Watching GitHub Actions run in the Actions tab, and seeing it go red once because your eval score dropped  
* Deploying, then hitting your live URL from your phone or another machine for the first time  
* Watching real request logs stream in once it's live  
* Pasting an actual stack trace to your AI tool and judging whether its proposed fix is right  
* Checking your API usage dashboard and seeing what tokens really cost in practice
